items.title: Building Reliable Tool-Using Agents
items.abstract:
Building Reliable Tool-Using Agents was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on the engineering of reliable agents, tool use, orchestration, and state management. The project referenced by this session is OpenHands/OpenHands. Programme notes describe the project as: An open platform that lets AI software agents write code, run commands, browse, and complete development tasks end to end. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Several examples show how to keep an agent grounded in an environment: sandboxed file systems, browser sessions, shell access, and structured observations that the model can verify.

The speaker opens with a taxonomy of agent runtimes: planners, executors, tool routers, memory services, and policy layers that decide when an autonomous loop should stop and ask for help.

The session compares single-agent loops with multi-agent topologies and argues that most production failures come from unclear handoffs rather than weak models.

The talk closes with cost and latency accounting, showing where orchestration overhead dominates and how caching, batching, and concurrency limits change the economics of agent products.

Observability receives a full section. The speaker demonstrates span-level traces that connect a user request to each planning step, tool invocation, retry, and final artifact.

The team presents a checklist for reliability: deterministic tool adapters, idempotent actions, checkpointed state, and replayable transcripts for every long-running task.

Method and measurement. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer.

Takeaways. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. The main takeaway is to measure the bottleneck before redesigning the architecture. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.

Session context. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. Several audience members asked for reproducible configurations, and the speaker pointed to the referenced project as the starting point. The session is part of a longer track on building dependable model applications for internal and external users.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

Multimodal RAG over Slides and Video was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on models that combine vision, language, and structured interfaces. The project referenced by this session is LLaVA-VL/LLaVA-NeXT. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source LLaVA-NeXT project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The closing section lists open problems in multimodal agents that must read, point, and act in the same environment.

The talk demonstrates human review loops that catch hallucinated chart values before model output reaches an executive dashboard.

The speaker compares captioning, grounding, and instruction-following objectives, noting that each objective produces different failure patterns.

Evaluation receives substantial attention, because multimodal benchmarks are easy to overfit and hard to reproduce across preprocessing pipelines.

Serving considerations include image preprocessing latency, cache keys for repeated media, and safe fallbacks when vision input is malformed.

Document understanding examples show why resolution, layout, and reading order matter more than raw parameter count for business documents.

Method and measurement. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer.

Takeaways. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.

The presentation assumes familiarity with Python and basic model-serving concepts but does not require research experience.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The session focuses on measurement, benchmarking, red-teaming, and guardrails for deployed models. The project referenced by this session is mlcommons/inference. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source inference project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The talk examines contamination, leakage, and benchmark saturation, with practical tests for detecting them before leaders rely on a score.

Safety filters are evaluated on both false positives and false negatives, because over-blocking quietly destroys user trust and product metrics.

The closing segment connects evaluation results to release decisions and rollback criteria.

The speaker starts from the observation that evaluation is a product requirement, not a research afterthought, and that ambiguous metrics create false confidence.

The speaker argues for reproducible evaluation artifacts: frozen datasets, versioned prompts, and recorded model snapshots.

The session distinguishes offline quality checks, online guardrails, and incident review, showing how each catches different failures.

Method and measurement. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces.

Takeaways. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. Questions about scale were answered with a reminder that the operational envelope matters more than the peak headline number.

Session context. Examples were drawn from internal tools, customer-facing assistants, and open-source deployments. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design. Slides, recordings, and short notes accompany the session in the archive.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.
